title: Specimen Days
description: Published in 1882 and Whitman's prose masterpiece: a diary-memoir of the war hospitals, the American landscape and the poet's old age.
plot_or_argument: Whitman records the wounded in the Washington hospitals, the death of Lincoln, his own strokes, the New Jersey countryside and the butterflies and birds of his garden at Camden, in a series of dated notes that build a portrait of a life.
historical_context: The 1862-82, the Civil War hospitals, the Camden years, and the American tradition of the diary and the sketch.
literary_significance: Specimen Days is the finest American prose memoir of the century and one of the great works of American nature writing: its war journal is the most truthful record of the Civil War hospitals, and its landscape notes made the American sketch a serious literary form.

title: 'Because I could not stop for Death'
description: Written about 1863 and first published in 1890: the single most famous American poem, in which Death comes as a gentleman caller and the speaker rides with him toward eternity.
plot_or_argument: The speaker is collected by Death and Immortality in a carriage; they pass the school, the fields and the setting sun, and arrive at a house that is a grave, and the poem ends with the recognition that the journey has lasted centuries.
meter_and_prosody: Six four-line ballad stanzas, mostly iambic tetrameter and trimeter, with slant rhyme.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Amherst of Dickinson's seclusion, the hymn tradition of New England, and the American civil religion of death.
literary_significance: 'Because I could not stop for Death' is the central poem of American literature and one of the greatest lyrics in English: its domestic allegory of death and its final image of eternity have made it the most anthologised American poem.

title: 'I heard a Fly buzz — when I died —'
description: Written about 1862 and first published in 1896: the deathbed scene in which the mourners wait for the King and the room is filled with the sound of a fly.
plot_or_argument: The speaker lies dying, the watchers have gathered, the wills and the keepsakes are divided, and at the moment of expectation — 'the Windows failed' — the fly intervenes and the poem ends in the blank light.
historical_context: The 1860s, the New England deathbed, the Calvinist expectation of salvation, and the American essay on death.
literary_significance: 'I heard a Fly buzz' is one of the greatest short poems in American literature and the central text of Dickinson's ironic theology: its refusal of consolation, and the fly that fills the place of God, make it a permanent challenge to the religious poetry of the century.

title: Poems by Emily Dickinson
description: Published in 1890, four years after her death, and the first selection of Dickinson's poems: 116 poems, heavily edited for punctuation and rhyme, which introduced her to the world.
plot_or_argument: The collection presents Dickinson's poems under the headings of Life, Nature, Love and Time and Eternity, and includes 'Success is counted sweetest', 'I'm Nobody! Who are you?', 'The Soul selects her own Society' and 'There's a certain Slant of light'.
literary_form: Poetry collection (posthumous, edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson)
historical_context: The 1890, the posthumous publication arranged by her sister Lavinia, the American magazine culture, and the Victorian editing of women's verse.
literary_significance: Poems by Emily Dickinson made one of the greatest poets in English known to the world and created the image of Dickinson as the reclusive Amherst lyricist; although the text was later restored, the 1890 edition is itself a central document in the history of American poetry and of the editing of women's writing.
attribution_notes: Posthumous edition by Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson, who regularised Dickinson's punctuation and rhyme; the restored texts appeared in 1955 and the manuscript facsimiles in 1981.

title: Poems, Second Series
description: Published in 1891 and the second posthumous selection: 166 poems, including 'I felt a Funeral, in my Brain', 'A narrow Fellow in the Grass' and 'The Brain — is wider than the Sky'.
plot_or_argument: The volume continues the arrangement of the first series and adds the poems of the inner life, of the snakes and the birds of Amherst, and of the mind's power, which are among the most metaphysical in American poetry.
historical_context: The 1891, the first reception of Dickinson, the American debate on her metre, and the Victorian editing of her texts.
literary_significance: Poems, Second Series deepened the first collection and made Dickinson's intellectual ambition unmistakable; together the two volumes established her as a major poet and set the terms of the critical debate that continues today.
attribution_notes: Posthumous edition by Todd and Higginson; the punctuation of the manuscripts differs substantially.

title: The Poems of Emily Dickinson (Johnson edition)
description: Published in 1955 and the first complete and restored edition of Dickinson's poems, edited by Thomas H. Johnson from the manuscripts and fascicles.
plot_or_argument: The edition restores the dashes, the capitalisation, the slant rhymes and the manuscript order of the poems, and prints all 1,775 poems in the sequence of their composition.
literary_form: Scholarly edition of the complete poems
historical_context: The 1955, the modern textual scholarship of American literature, and the recovery of women's writing in the twentieth century.
literary_significance: The Johnson edition made the real Dickinson available and is the foundation of all modern Dickinson criticism: it restored the poems that the 1890s editors had regularised, and it established her as the central American woman poet and one of the greatest poets in English.

title: Uncle Tom's Cabin; or, Life among the Lowly
description: Serialised in the National Era from June 1851 and published in two volumes in March 1852: the most influential novel ever published in the United States.
plot_or_argument: Uncle Tom, a pious enslaved man in Kentucky, is sold south with the child Harry, whose mother Eliza escapes across the ice of the Ohio River; Tom is bought by the saintly Eva St Clare, then sold to the brutal Simon Legree, and dies refusing to reveal the hiding place of two enslaved women, while George and Eliza escape to Canada and freedom.
principal_characters: Uncle Tom; Eliza Harris; George Harris; Harry; Eva St Clare; Augustine St Clare; Simon Legree; Cassy; Emmeline; Topsy; Miss Ophelia; Chloe
historical_context: The 1850-52, the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850, the abolitionist movement, and the American debate on slavery that led to the Civil War.
literary_significance: Uncle Tom's Cabin is the central American novel of slavery and the most politically effective novel ever written: it converted hundreds of thousands to abolitionism, made Uncle Tom and Simon Legree permanent figures of the language, and is the founding text of the American literature of human rights.

title: Dred: A Tale of the Great Dismal Swamp
description: Published in 1856 and Stowe's second anti-slavery novel, and the more radical of the two: the story of a fugitive insurrectionary in the Great Dismal Swamp and of the southern families he haunts.
plot_or_argument: Dred, the son of the rebel Denmark Vesey, lives as a fugitive in the swamp and preaches a coming judgement on slavery; the novel follows the decline of the Peyton family, the villainy of the lawyer Jekyl and of Tom Gordon, and the fates of the enslaved families who are separated and sold.
historical_context: The 1856, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the rise of the Republican Party, and the American debate on the possibility of slave insurrection.
literary_significance: Dred is the central American novel of slave rebellion and the most radical of Stowe's books: it is the first American novel to make an insurrectionary black hero the centre of its moral vision, and it is a key text in the literature of slavery and resistance.

title: The Minister's Wooing
description: Published in 1859 and Stowe's finest novel of New England: a story of Calvinist theology, the sea and a woman's conscience in Newport, Rhode Island.
plot_or_argument: Mary Scudder, a young woman of Newport, is loved by the minister Dr Hopkins and by the sailor James Marvyn, who is lost at sea; the novel's real subject is the Calvinist doctrine of election and the agony it produces in a devout and loving woman.
historical_context: The 1850s, New England Congregationalism after Edwards, the slave trade in Rhode Island, and the American theological debate on the atonement.
literary_significance: The Minister's Wooing is the finest American novel of New England religious life and the great Stowe novel of the Calvinist conscience: its portrait of Mary Scudder and its analysis of the doctrine of election are unmatched in American fiction.

title: Oldtown Folks
description: Published in 1869 and Stowe's most autobiographical novel: the childhood of two orphans in a Massachusetts village, and a portrait of New England life after the Revolution.
plot_or_argument: Horace Holyoke and his cousins grow up in the village of Oldtown among ministers, deacons, farmers and spinsters, and the novel records the customs, the theology and the humour of the New England of Stowe's own childhood.
historical_context: The 1790s-1800s, post-Revolutionary New England, the Congregational ministry, and the American village in the early republic.
literary_significance: Oldtown Folks is the finest American regional novel of New England and the great fictional record of the New England village culture that produced both Stowe and the American Renaissance; its portrait of the Calvinist community is a central document of American social history.

title: Poganuc People: Their Loves and Lives
description: Published in 1878 and Stowe's last New England novel: the life of a Connecticut village and of the clergyman's daughter Dolly, drawn closely from her own childhood at Litchfield.
plot_or_argument: Dolly, the daughter of the minister of Poganuc, grows up among the parties, the sleigh rides, the revivals and the social distinctions of a small Connecticut town, and the novel ends with her coming of age and the departure of the old order.
historical_context: The 1830s, Connecticut Congregationalism, the Second Great Awakening, and the American village before the railroad.
literary_significance: Poganuc People is the most charming of Stowe's New England books and a key text in the American literature of the village; its record of the religious revivals and the social life of the 1830s is a primary document of American culture.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
description: Published in 1845 in Boston and the founding text of the African-American literary tradition: the account of Douglass's life from his birth in slavery to his escape and his first years of freedom.
plot_or_argument: Douglass records his separation from his mother, the cruelty of the overseer Covey, his learning to read, his fight with Covey, his escape disguised as a sailor, and his arrival in New Bedford, and ends with his first speech at Nantucket.
historical_context: The 1818-45, the slave economy of Maryland, the abolitionist movement, and the American debate on the reliability of slave testimony.
literary_significance: The Narrative is the central American slave narrative and the founding text of African-American literature: its account of literacy, resistance and escape set the pattern for the genre, and its eloquence made Douglass the most important black voice in the English-speaking world.

title: 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?'
description: Delivered at Rochester on 5 July 1852 and published the same year: the greatest American political speech of the nineteenth century, and the most complete indictment of American hypocrisy.
plot_or_argument: Douglass tells his audience that the Fourth of July is not his, that the slave's wrongs are shared by every American, and that the republic's professions of liberty are mocked by the slave market in the capital; he ends with a call to abolish slavery and to make the Declaration true.
historical_context: The 1852, the Fugitive Slave Law, the abolitionist movement, and the American celebration of the Fourth of July.
literary_significance: The Fourth of July address is the central American oration and the founding text of the black critique of American democracy: its phrases have entered the language, and it remains the most powerful statement of the gap between American ideals and American practice.

title: My Bondage and My Freedom
description: Published in 1855 and the second and fullest of Douglass's autobiographies: an expanded account of slavery and freedom that includes his break with Garrison and his own analysis of the slave system.
plot_or_argument: Douglass adds to the 1845 narrative the account of his childhood, the death of his mother, the economics of the plantation, his escape, his early years as an abolitionist, his travels in Britain and Ireland, and his purchase of his freedom.
historical_context: The 1855, the split in the abolitionist movement between Garrison and the political abolitionists, and the American debate on the Constitution and slavery.
literary_significance: My Bondage and My Freedom is the greatest of the slave narratives and the most analytically powerful: its account of slavery as an economic system and its argument for political abolition made it the central text of black political thought before the Civil War.

title: The Heroic Slave
description: Published in 1853 and the only work of fiction Douglass wrote: a novella based on the revolt led by Madison Washington aboard the slave ship Creole in 1841.
plot_or_argument: Madison Washington, an enslaved Virginian who has escaped to Canada, returns to rescue his wife and is shipped to New Orleans; he leads the seizure of the Creole and sails the ship to Nassau, where the British free the rebels.
historical_context: The 1841, the Creole case, the British abolition of slavery in the colonies, and the American debate on the legal status of slave revolt.
literary_significance: The Heroic Slave is the first American work of fiction by a black writer and the founding text of African-American fiction: it invented the black revolutionary hero of American literature and made the slave revolt a subject of the American imagination.

title: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
description: Published in 1881 and revised in 1892: the last and longest of Douglass's autobiographies, covering the Civil War, emancipation and the disappointments of Reconstruction.
plot_or_argument: Douglass recounts his escape, his abolitionist career, his recruitment of black troops in the Civil War, his meetings with Lincoln, his service as marshal of the District of Columbia and minister to Haiti, and his growing despair at the betrayal of the freedpeople.
historical_context: The 1881-92, the Civil War and Reconstruction, the withdrawal of federal troops in 1877, the rise of Jim Crow, and the American debate on the Negro problem.
literary_significance: Life and Times is the central American autobiography of the nineteenth century and the fullest record of the black experience from slavery to the nadir of race relations: it is the essential document of Reconstruction and of the failure of American emancipation.

title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself
description: Published in 1861 under the pseudonym Linda Brent and the first full-length slave narrative by a woman: the account of Harriet Jacobs's life in slavery and of her seven years hiding in a garret.
plot_or_argument: Linda Brent is pursued by her master Dr Flint, becomes the mother of two children by a white lawyer, hides for seven years in a tiny garret above her grandmother's shed, escapes to the North, and after the Fugitive Slave Law is forced to hide again; she is finally freed and works as a nurse.
literary_form: Autobiography (slave narrative; published as Linda Brent, edited by Lydia Maria Child)
historical_context: The 1820s-50s, the slave society of Edenton, North Carolina, the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850, and the abolitionist movement.
literary_significance: Incidents is a founding text of African-American women's writing and of American autobiography: it is the first slave narrative to make the sexual exploitation of enslaved women its central subject, and its seven-year hiding is one of the most extraordinary acts of resistance in American history.

title: Letters and Relief Work among the Freedpeople
description: Written between 1862 and 1868 while Jacobs worked among the freedpeople of Alexandria and Savannah, and published in the American Freedman and the abolitionist press.
plot_or_argument: Jacobs describes the condition of the refugees, the schools, the hospitals, the treatment of the women and children, and the obstacles placed in the way of the freedpeople by the army and by the government.
historical_context: The 1862-68, the Civil War and Reconstruction, the contraband camps, and the Freedmen's Bureau.
literary_significance: Jacobs's relief work and reports are a significant primary document of Reconstruction and of the freedpeople's experience, and they extend her literary achievement into the history of American social reform.

title: Lady Audley's Secret
description: Serialised in 1861-62 and published in three volumes: the most successful of all English sensation novels, and the one that made the beauties of the genre into a serious argument about the law.
plot_or_argument: Robert Audley investigates the disappearance of his friend George Talboys and comes to suspect that his uncle's beautiful young wife, Lady Audley, is George's supposedly dead wife Helen; he pursues her through a series of disguises to a private asylum in Belgium, and the novel ends with her confession and her retirement to a maison de sante, and with Robert's marriage to Clara Talboys.
principal_characters: Lady Audley (Helen Talboys); Robert Audley; George Talboys; Sir Michael Audley; Alicia Audley; Clara Talboys; Luke Marks; Phoebe Marks; Dr Mosgrave
literary_form: Sensation novel (serialised in Robin Goodfellow and the Sixpenny Magazine, 1861-62; three volumes 1862)
historical_context: The 1860s, the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, the private lunatic asylum trade, and the circulating-library market for three-volume fiction.
literary_significance: Lady Audley's Secret is the central English sensation novel and one of the most important Victorian novels about the legal and social position of women: its heroine's crime is the logical response to a world in which a poor woman has no legal existence of her own, and the novel's use of the asylum to silence her is a direct indictment of Victorian psychiatry.

title: Aurora Floyd
description: Published in 1863 and Braddon's second great sensation novel: the story of an heiress with a violent temper, a secret marriage and a husband who may return at any moment.
plot_or_argument: Aurora Floyd, the daughter of a banker, secretly marries the groom James Conyers and pays him to disappear; she later marries the landowner John Mellish, and Conyers's return leads to his murder, the trial of Mellish, and the eventual discovery that the killer is Aurora's cousin's husband.
principal_characters: Aurora Floyd; John Mellish; Talbot Bulstrode; James Conyers; Lucy Floyd; Archibald Floyd; Matthew Harrison; Eliza
historical_context: The 1860s, the horse-racing and betting world, the railway, and the marriage law.
literary_significance: Aurora Floyd is the fullest sensation treatment of the woman with a secret past and one of the earliest English novels to give a heroine an aggressive, physical energy — riding, hunting, fighting — that the period associated with men.

title: The Doctor's Wife
description: Published in 1864 and a deliberate English answer to Flaubert's Madame Bovary: the story of a doctor's wife whose reading of novels fills her with romantic expectations her marriage cannot satisfy.
plot_or_argument: Isabel Sleaford marries the good, dull country doctor George Gilbert, is courted in imagination by the fashionable novelist Roland Lansdell, and drifts into an emotional affair; the death of her mother and her husband's forbearance bring her back to her marriage, which ends in the ordinary happiness of a life accepted.
historical_context: The 1860s, the circulating-library novel and its female readers, the medical profession, and the English reception of French realism.
literary_significance: The Doctor's Wife is the most self-conscious English novel about the novel-reading woman: it takes the French realist diagnosis of romantic reading and turns it into a defence of English domestic life, and it is a key text for the history of the woman reader.

title: Uncle Silas: A Tale of Bartram-Haugh
description: Published in 1864 and the finest of Le Fanu's novels: the story of a young heiress left in the power of her sinister uncle in a remote Derbyshire house.
plot_or_argument: Maud Ruthyn, whose father has made her uncle Silas her guardian, goes to Bartram-Haugh, where Silas — a ruined gambler suspected of the murder of a moneylender — and his governess Madame de la Rougierre conspire to marry her to Silas's son Dudley and, when that fails, to murder her; she escapes with the help of her cousin Monica and the servant Mary Quince.
principal_characters: Maud Ruthyn; Silas Ruthyn; Austin Ruthyn; Madame de la Rougierre; Dudley Ruthyn; Monica Knollys; Mary Quince; Godfrey Knollys; Dr Bryerly; Tom Brice
historical_context: The 1860s, the power of a guardian under English law, the private asylum and the fortune-hunting of the impoverished gentry.
literary_significance: Uncle Silas is the greatest English novel of suspense before the 1890s and the finest single achievement of the Irish Gothic: its portrait of a charming, hypocritical villain and of a young woman's isolation is unmatched in Victorian fiction, and it was a model for Henry James and for the modern thriller.

title: Carmilla
description: Published in the collection In a Glass Darkly in 1872 and the founding text of the lesbian vampire narrative: the story of a young woman in Styria who is visited by a beautiful guest who is not alive.
plot_or_argument: Laura, the daughter of a retired Austrian officer, is visited as a child and then as a young woman by Carmilla, who is in fact the revenant of the Countess Mircalla Karnstein; Laura weakens, a peasant girl dies, and Baron Vordenburg traces the vampire to the ruined chapel of Karnstein, where she is destroyed.
narrative_structure: A first-person memoir framed by the case notes of Dr Martin Hesselius.
principal_characters: Laura; Carmilla (Mircalla, Countess Karnstein); General Spielsdorf; Baron Vordenburg; Laura's father; Bertha Rheinfeldt; Madame Perrodon
historical_context: The 1870s, the Austrian frontier and its folklore, the Gothic tradition of the vampire from Polidori, and the Victorian medical discourse on hysteria.
literary_significance: Carmilla is the most influential vampire story before Dracula and the origin of the female vampire in English literature; its treatment of an intense attachment between two women has made it the founding text of the queer Gothic.

title: The House by the Churchyard
description: Published in 1863 and the strangest of Le Fanu's long novels: a mystery of eighteenth-century Dublin and Chapelizod, built on a buried body, a disputed will and a ghost.
plot_or_argument: The novel moves between the garrison town of Chapelizod and the Dublin of the 1760s, where the murder of a man in the churchyard, the fate of the beautiful Miss Gertrude Chattesworth and the schemes of the sinister Dangerfield are gradually explained.
historical_context: The 1760s, the Dublin garrison, the Irish Protestant gentry, and the Irish folklore of the banshee and the haunted churchyard.
literary_significance: The House by the Churchyard is Le Fanu's most Irish book and the fullest fictional picture of eighteenth-century Dublin life; it influenced Joyce, who cited it in Finnegans Wake, and it is a key text in the Irish regional novel.

title: The Cloister and the Hearth: A Tale of the Middle Ages
description: Published in 1861 and the greatest English historical novel of the Middle Ages: the story of Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou, who travels from Holland to Rome in the fifteenth century in search of the woman he loves, and becomes the father of Erasmus.
plot_or_argument: Gerard, an illuminator's son, loves Margaret Brandt but is driven from home by his father; he travels through Burgundy, France and Italy, is imprisoned, joins a company of soldiers and survives a series of picaresque adventures, while Margaret bears his son and dies before his return; Gerard becomes a priest and the novel ends with the boy Erasmus at the age of reason.
principal_characters: Gerard Eliassoen; Margaret Brandt; Denys the soldier; Catherine Elias; Elias the printer; Ghysbrecht van Swieten; Cornelis and Sybrandt; Clement the hermit
historical_context: The 1450s-70s, the Burgundian Netherlands, the eve of the Reformation, and the medieval illuminated manuscript.
literary_significance: The Cloister and the Hearth is the classic English historical novel of the fifteenth century and the one Victorian book that attempts a full material reconstruction of medieval life — food, costume, trade, disease and travel; its portrait of a pre-Reformation world on the edge of change shaped the historical novel for a century.
